review.summary: The strongest findings are on the host side, not an isolate escape. The MCP request chooses the namespace used for project controls and retry accounting; rejected tool results can disclose information without a provenance tag; and the reviewer can give the same verdict to outputs of different types because its input erases the distinction. The first review's F2, F3, F4 and F9 fixes are partial. I did not establish arbitrary host code execution, access to the verification key from a script, or a production route to invoke an unclassified tool. This is a source review, not a deployed-runtime test.

findings.where: mcpAdapter's run callback, mcpResponse, productionAttempts, exposureFor
findings.title: The model chooses the namespace that is supposed to contain its failures
findings.detail: Authentication establishes the owner, but the project passed to attemptsFor, noticesFor and the service is the tool argument. There is no project binding in McpCaller. A different project selects a different attempt key, pause state and quota namespace. An absent project defaults to public rather than being rejected by exposureFor. This matters even with one owner: the threat model includes an owner's model acting on planted instructions. This does not bypass the installation kill switch, provider ceiling or tier checks, and it is not evidence of impersonating another owner.
findings.proof: In the adapter, the same authenticated principal and two different project arguments select two different attemptKey(principal.id, project) values. A closed first gate therefore does not close the second. A service-level test should also establish whether unknown project IDs are rejected by any omitted control before admission or execution.
findings.fix: Bind the active project to trusted session or task state. Require an existing, authorized project before reading notices, looking up attempts or charging quotas. If project switching is intentional, add a caller-wide abuse limit and do not treat a model-supplied switch as a new trusted task.

findings.where: brokerHost.accept and callTool's catch around accept; check
findings.title: Rejected results can disclose upstream data without counting as reads
findings.detail: The first review's F4 fix covers an exception from deps.upstream, but not an exception while accepting its result. An oversize result exposes its exact serialized size. An output schema that rejects unlisted properties can put an upstream-controlled property name in the error. callTool rethrows that error without sensitive-error redaction or a reads entry. A script can receive information from a sensitive tool while the broker still regards the run as having read nothing.
findings.proof: Use a fake sensitive upstream whose output has an unexpected field with a harmless canary name and whose output schema forbids additional properties. The validation diagnostic includes the canary, but accept throws before reads.push. This is source-visible; no assumption about transport of nested error causes is necessary.
findings.fix: Treat diagnostics derived from upstream results as upstream data. For sensitive tools return fixed errors without field names or exact sizes. Tag any diagnostic that is delivered before handing it across the bridge. Apply one error-disclosure policy to both invocation and result validation.

findings.where: RUNNER_SOURCE: Code.run, assert, assertionReport, critical and final serialization
findings.title: The runner shares mutable JavaScript machinery with the script whose behavior it reports
findings.detail: The wrapper separates lexical variables, not realms. After script execution, the runner uses ambient JSON, array and string operations to produce evidence about that execution. The static check rejects reassignment of global identifiers, not mutation of their properties. There is also a sequencing flaw independent of global mutation: serializing a returned object can execute script-defined serialization behavior after the last failedAssertion check. If an assertion fails and is caught during that step, the completed path does not check the latch again. These are integrity failures inside the isolate, not evidence of host execution.
findings.proof: A runner regression test should arrange for a caught assertion failure during serialization of an otherwise ordinary final value. The required outcome is assertion_failed. The current completed path tests failedAssertion only before JSON.stringify. Separately, verify that changes to script-visible serialization facilities cannot change how runner-owned declarations are encoded.
findings.fix: Separate script evaluation from trusted evidence collection. Capture and harden required intrinsics before execution; do not invoke script-owned serialization hooks on runner-owned evidence. Close the tool-call capability before finalization, and check the failure latch after every finalization step that can execute guest code.

findings.title: A reviewer pass can attest to a different output than the caller receives
findings.detail: reviewMaterial leaves strings alone but converts all other outputs to JSON text. This erases distinctions necessary to judge type-sensitive criteria. The run also sends the result but not the released logs, and a long result is judged from a prefix. The code accepts a pass on a prefix even though only the prompt says an incomplete view cannot satisfy a criterion.
findings.proof: With the same report and criterion 'the result is the number 5', reviewMaterial produces identical material for the number 5 and the string "5". No reviewer, however capable, can reliably distinguish those cases. The existing right-number golden case tests only one of the pair.
findings.fix: Preserve JSON types in review material. Define what a pass covers: include all released fields covered by the criteria, or label the verdict as result-only. Make incomplete review material ineligible for a full pass in code. Add the number/string pair as golden cases.

findings.where: HostBridge.callTool, countingHost.callTool, RUNNER_SOURCE error and result reporting
findings.title: Guest CPU and output limits do not bound the work bought in the host
findings.detail: The first review's F3 fix reduces normal result and log traffic. It does not limit tool arguments at bridge entry. countingHost serializes and UTF-8 encodes arguments before the broker even looks up the tool. An allowed call can be serialized again for data-flow accounting. Separately, the runner builds the entire final JSON before cutting it, and ordinary script error messages have no runner-side cap before RPC. The host's later message truncation is not a transport limit.
findings.proof: The first size check for journal arguments occurs after byteLength(args) has allocated the serialization. MAX_LOGGED_ARGUMENT_BYTES limits retention, not work. On the return path, the ordinary error branch puts String((error && error.message) || error) directly into the report. The platform's RPC maximum, not supplied here, determines the largest single transfer.
findings.fix: Use a bounded data-only wire format with byte, depth and aggregate per-run limits. Enforce transport limits before host deserialization where supported, and reject oversized envelopes before journaling or schema traversal. Bound every report field before RPC, including errors. Measure peak host memory as well as final output size.

findings.title: Quota reservations are not safe under concurrent calls or day rollover
findings.detail: Sibling calls share a mutable ahead object. A reservation awaits countCall with one block size but then sets ahead.left from the current ahead.block, which another continuation may have changed. The number of local credits can therefore differ from the number reserved. In addition, credits have no window identity: close refunds them using the time of return, not the time of reservation. A refund just after midnight can lower the new day's count for calls reserved the previous day.
findings.proof: A deterministic unit test can suspend two countCall operations for the same path and complete them separately, comparing store reservations to credits consumed and refunded. A separate fake-clock test can reserve before a UTC day boundary and close just after it. returnCalls explicitly selects the latter window.
findings.fix: Serialize reservation changes per tool and give each reservation an immutable amount and window ID. Consume or refund only credits from that reservation. Coordinate close with pending reservations.

findings.title: Discovery can continue spending host resources after the run closes
findings.detail: First-review F2 added a useful guard immediately before tool dispatch and after its result. Discovery does not have equivalent guards after awaits. search can list the entire policy table, then fetch documentation once per eligible path, including after a timeout or sibling denial. The F9 query-length and word limits do not limit records scanned, document bytes, lookups or results. describe can likewise return documentation after closure.
findings.proof: Pause a fake store.list, close the broker, then resolve list with eligible records. The search loop has no guard before docsFor or before returning. One short query still initiates work proportional to the catalog. The current small GitHub catalog limits practical impact, not the implementation.
findings.fix: Bound discovery by an indexed candidate limit, document bytes, result count and per-run work budget. Recheck closure after waits and propagate cancellation to backing reads where supported.

findings.title: One unavailable golden case discards a demonstrated reviewer failure
findings.detail: runGoldenCheck computes wrong but returns 'nothing counted' if any other case was not asked. A day with a known wrong verdict is thus equated with a day with no evidence. The daily check also uses the same installation-wide budget as ordinary reviews. Exhaustion does not by itself switch a healthy reviewer off, but it can suppress failure evidence or prevent an already-disabled reviewer from demonstrating recovery. claimDay prevents another check that day.
findings.proof: With a fake reviewer, return a wrong readable verdict for one golden case and reviewer_refused for another. No failed day is recorded. If the reviewer was off, budget refusals also leave it off. Neither outcome requires manipulating the actual model.
findings.fix: Count a demonstrated wrong verdict as a failed check even if other cases were unavailable. Require all cases for a pass. Reserve a small independent budget for health checks, record incomplete days separately, and permit a bounded retry of incomplete checks.

findings.title: The verification reply byte limit is applied after buffering and in the wrong units
findings.detail: The host awaits response.text() before checking maxReplyBytes. This buffers the whole provider response, and raw.length then measures UTF-16 code units, not wire or decoded UTF-8 bytes. max_output_tokens constrains requested model output, not the size of the complete HTTP response.
findings.proof: A fake provider response containing multibyte text can exceed the stated byte ceiling while passing the character-count check. Even a response subsequently rejected is fully read first. This is a provider-response boundary; I found no direct way for a guest to choose the response bytes.
findings.fix: Read the response stream with a cumulative byte limit, cancel on overflow, then decode and parse only the accepted bytes. Treat Content-Length as an early rejection hint, not the sole control.

findings.where: runOnce review input construction and reviewMaterial
findings.title: Verification classifies the tool reads, not the full material sent to the provider
findings.detail: The provider check receives read ?? "public", but the payload also contains caller-supplied intent, criteria, report fields and a result that can include caller-supplied literals. No tool read is required for those to contain nonpublic information. The provider ceiling is correctly enforced against the supplied label; the label does not establish that the entire payload meets it. In particular, a closed client-personal-data gate is not an outbound content guarantee.
findings.proof: A no-tool run with criteria causes the review request to be labelled public regardless of the project's class or the contents of intent and criteria. This follows directly from the call site. Actual disclosure depends on what callers put in those fields and whether the omitted ingress layer enforces a classification contract.
findings.fix: Derive the outbound classification from all inputs to review, using trusted request/project classification as a floor in addition to tool provenance. Minimize report fields sent to the reviewer and skip external review if the full payload cannot be classified for that route.

findings.where: callTool's checkDataFlow, checkQuotas and final guard
findings.title: Outbound authorization is checked before an asynchronous gap in which provenance can change
findings.detail: checkDataFlow decides whether the run has read sensitive data before awaiting quota storage. A sibling read can be accepted during that wait. The final guard checks only closed and ended, not the data-flow condition. Thus the stated rule that an outbound dispatch after a sensitive read requires an approved destination does not hold at dispatch time. This is not proof that arguments already fixed before the read can contain its result, and the stated Phase 1 connector set limits the consequence.
findings.proof: A fake quota store can suspend a permitted outbound call after checkDataFlow. Accept a sensitive sibling read, then release the quota wait. The final guard sees an open run and does not inspect reads.
findings.fix: Enforce the sensitive-read condition again immediately before dispatch using immutable validated arguments, or serialize sensitive-read and outbound admission decisions. Keep diagnostic flagging separate so a second check does not double-count it.

checked_and_sound: First review F1: the refusal path still passes script text to audit.record. The earlier record says the audit layer redacts it and has a regression test; that layer is absent here, so this is neither a newly confirmed leak nor an independently reverified fix.

First review F2: close is forwarded through countingHost, and callTool checks guard immediately before upstream dispatch and before delivering a successful result. This does not cancel a request already dispatched. Discovery is the remaining gap described in F7.
First review F3: normal log collection is capped beside the script and normal result text is cut before RPC. This is a real improvement, not a general transport or allocation bound.

First review F4: the top-level message for sensitive invocation failures is replaced with fixed text and an optional bounded status. Non-sensitive invocation error text is tagged before it is thrown. Rejected results are the separate gap in F2.
First review F5: the schema checker collects located values from every passing anyOf branch; branch order no longer suppresses an otherwise applicable URL or path check.

First review F6: for the string-named properties the stripping pass examines, a remaining forbidden property prevents script invocation, and the host rejects a missing or nonempty globalsLeft list. This is not proof that every runtime capability is unreachable.

First review F7: unrecognized executor failures return fixed caller-facing text and keep platform detail separate for audit. First review F8: a masked run zeros the passed-assertion count. It does not eliminate the previously acknowledged metadata channels.
First review F9: query length, name length and query-word limits are present. They bound request shape but not catalog-dependent backend work.

Missing policy records, unusable stored records, direct-only tools, and nonzero tiers are refused in the shown call path. Both MCP tool forms use the same service. No fallback runs guest source in the host.

In production MCP, client-supplied model labels do not raise the provider ceiling. The reviewer verdict parser rejects malformed and contradictory verdicts, and the base reviewer does not convert a tier-2 pass into approval. These controls do not depend on the model following its prompt.
The verification credential is used for the fixed provider request, not included in review material or usage records. No direct credential disclosure to a guest was established.
not_reviewable_from_source: Cloudflare isolate confinement, RPC transport size limits, supported argument types, cancellation behavior, and whether a thrown Error's nested cause crosses RPC. The broker attaches the original cause even to the sanitized sensitive error; remove it at the boundary or confirm with a deployed harmless-canary test that it cannot cross.

The top-level host router, Access principal verification, any additional project authorization in service wiring, connector repository scoping, token cache isolation, redirect handling, and actual GitHub installation permissions.

Atomicity of storedAttemptGate and the production D1 stores. Concurrent MCP requests obtain separate gates before running; whether their settlements lose increments or reopen a closed gate requires the omitted implementation and a concurrency test.

Audit redaction, log access and retention; the releaseGate implementation and whether a final whole-envelope check covers report fields and adapter-added notices as well as result, logs and error message.

Registry hashing, connector implementation integrity, dependency provenance and deployed artifact identity. Comparing a pin with a definition sourced from the same build does not independently verify the build or connector behavior.

The reviewer's actual resistance to semantic prompt injection, the provider's real pricing and billing bounds, and whether the test Worker is running the reviewed commit. Escaped delimiters establish a formatting property, not model behavior.
